questions.explanation: #1 says it understands the concerns about ZCG, but argues the fund has served its purpose and that eliminating ZCG while leaving everything to coinholders fails to address taxation without representation. #1 and #3 say the problem is structure and incentives, not people, and #1 explicitly opposes the ZCG-only proposal, which is the third option.
options: The fund has been looted by its administrators and the committee is corrupt, so it must be shut down at once and its money returned to coinholders.
The fund has served its purpose and coinholder-controlled funding is taxation without representation, so ending only ZCG is a half-measure.
ZCG should be eliminated while the coinholder fund is kept at 100%, because coinholders have shown better judgment than any elected committee has.
Miners should receive all block rewards immediately, because the protocol does not allow coinholder votes to decide how issuance is spent.
questions.prompt: Which description of the case made in #1 for ending the Development Fund is accurate rather than a caricature?

questions.explanation: #6 turns the premise around: if purchasable stake is disqualifying, all coinholder votes on Zcash's direction would have to go, and it proposes node-based freedoms like Bitcoin's instead. joshs did not answer, so the claim stays contested. The wrong options attribute to #6 defenses of ZCG or of proof-of-work that it did not make.
options: By arguing that buying stake cannot work in a proof-of-work chain, so Steem's experience says nothing about the risks for Zcash or its funding.
By accepting the risk but saying that ZCG's five-member elected structure already protects the fund against any purchased influence at all.
By saying the attack is only dangerous for the ZCG slice of the fund, so coinholders should keep full control over the entire fund instead.
By noting that the same attack applies to every coinholder vote, so the logic would abolish them all, and suggesting node-based options such as UASFs.
questions.prompt: How did #6 respond to the argument that stake-based power can be bought, for example by a nation-state buying ZEC?

questions.explanation: #2 asks 'Who are they?' and says the election controversy's allegations were aimed at FPF and enforced by the community, not ZCG. #3 replies that what was communicated concerns past, not current, committees and that the structure is the problem, without naming anyone. Neither side concedes, which is why the claim is contested rather than unanswered or confirmed.
options: It was confirmed by named current grantees, and nobody in the thread disputed what those grantees said about their fear of speaking out.
It was conceded by its author after #2 showed that the fear of speaking out had never actually been reported to anyone by any grantee.
It was challenged in #2, which asked who the people are, and #3 narrowed it to past ZCG committees without naming anyone, so it stays contested.
It went unanswered, because no later post in the thread mentioned the fear of speaking out, the election controversy or any bans at all.
questions.prompt: Which statement about the claim that the fund structure quells speech is accurate?

questions.explanation: #13 gives ECC's Founders' Reward and Dev Fund amounts, compares them with the largest ZCG grantee, and quotes ZODL's own statement that the entire ECC team moved over. It does not claim ZODL won coinholder grants or misspent its raise. #17 does not dispute the figures; it says ZODL took no ECC resources.
options: A list of ZODL staff who earlier served on the ZCG committee, together with the grants those members approved for ZODL's earlier work and products.
Receipts of about 1.8M ZEC (Founders' Reward) and 367,500 ZEC (Dev Fund), versus the largest ZCG grantee's ~$5.8M, and ZODL saying the ECC team moved over.
Audited accounts showing ZODL spent its $25M seed round on salaries and marketing instead of on protocol development work for the network.
A tally showing ZODL had won most of the retroactive grants decided by quarterly coinholder votes since the fund structure was ratified in code.
questions.prompt: What evidence did #13 offer for the claim that ZODL continues ECC, the largest dev fund recipient to date?

questions.explanation: #1 combines taxation without representation, the incentive to optimize for the vote, and the point that large holders can simply write a check; #19 and #20 restate the representation point. The fund has not run out (#1 cites over $300M), and nobody argued that miners are uniquely trustworthy or that holders stopped voting.
options: Everyone is taxed but a few large holders choose the winners, teams optimize for the vote, and willing large holders can simply fund projects directly.
The fund has run out of money, so there is nothing left for anyone to govern and the committees can simply be closed down without further debate.
Ending the fund would send the rewards to miners, who are the only group that has never misused any funds that were meant for development work.
Large holders have stopped voting in the quarterly process, so it no longer works and the remaining money would otherwise be wasted by default.
questions.prompt: Which is the strongest case actually made in the thread for ending the Development Fund entirely?

questions.explanation: #13 argues that the fund helped build ZODL and that new teams deserve the same chance, so the answer to misaligned incentives is a neutral, transparent system rather than ending the fund; #11 adds that private funding is not yet plentiful. The first option reverses their point, and nobody argued the legal or paid-critics points.
options: Private investors will fill the gap immediately once the fund stops, so any restructuring of the fund can safely wait until some later point.
The accrued money cannot legally be redirected under the existing ZIPs, so the fund must simply continue untouched and unchanged until 2028.
New teams may have no other path, and misaligned incentives call for a transparent, neutral funding system, since Zcash needs more teams, not fewer.
Critics of the fund are paid by competitors, so their arguments can be set aside and the existing structure left exactly as it is for now.
questions.prompt: Which is the strongest case actually made in the thread for keeping a fund but restructuring it instead of ending it?

questions.explanation: #23 argues that voting only with money disenfranchises less wealthy holders and asks for coinholder-person polling alongside coinholder-amount polling. #24 adds that polling is an information input, not a binding vote, and that non-coinholders must count too; #11 and #26 make related points. None of them argued for ZCG-only decisions or for weighting larger holders more.
options: Coinholders should have no say over development funding at all, and every decision should be made only by ZCG's elected committee instead.
Votes should be weighted even more heavily toward the largest holders, since they carry the most financial risk if the network ever fails.
Polling should be dropped in favor of binding majority votes, because polls cannot be trusted as a reliable source of information at all.
Voting by coin amount lets wealth decide and excludes poorer holders and non-coinholders; per-person polling should be added as one input among several.
questions.prompt: Which description matches what #23 and #24 hold about coinholder voting?

questions.explanation: #17 answers with ZODL's own position: it is unprofitable, ending the fund hurts it financially, he refused direct dev funding as ECC CEO, and the raise aimed to remove dependence on the fund. It does not dispute the figures or the licensing changes in #13, so those points remain unanswered. The other options invent responses that #17 did not give.
options: By saying ZODL is unprofitable and ending the fund hurts it too, that he refused direct dev funding as ECC CEO, and that he acts against his own interest.
By disputing the 1.8M ZEC and 367,500 ZEC figures and saying the amounts ECC actually received were far smaller than #13 states them to be.
By agreeing that ZODL should step back from the debate and let the teams that still need the fund set the proposal for what comes next.
By arguing that the Bootstrap IP purchase was paid out of Dev Fund money, so ZODL had already returned what it had earlier received from it.
questions.prompt: How did #17 respond to the argument that ZODL, as the biggest past recipient, is structurally misaligned to propose ending the fund?
